Fitted and predicted values of mcp models fits

Source: R/predict.R
execute-mcp-model.Rd

Evaluate the model on data, either summarised (per data-row) or per draw. You can use draws from the prior (prior = TRUE), select a distributional parameter with dpar, and choose the response or linear-predictor scale with scale where applicable. See Fits and predictions for worked examples, including forecasts with future change points.

Usage

# S3 method for class 'mcpfit'
predict(
  object,
  newdata = NULL,
  summary = TRUE,
  width = 0.95,
  rate = FALSE,
  prior = FALSE,
  group_effects = TRUE,
  arma = TRUE,
  ndraws = NULL,
  draws_format = "tidy",
  nsamples = lifecycle::deprecated(),
  samples_format = lifecycle::deprecated(),
  varying = lifecycle::deprecated(),
  probs = lifecycle::deprecated(),
  ...
)

# S3 method for class 'mcpfit'
fitted(
  object,
  newdata = NULL,
  summary = TRUE,
  width = 0.95,
  rate = FALSE,
  prior = FALSE,
  dpar = "epred",
  group_effects = TRUE,
  arma = TRUE,
  ndraws = NULL,
  draws_format = "tidy",
  scale = "response",
  nsamples = lifecycle::deprecated(),
  samples_format = lifecycle::deprecated(),
  varying = lifecycle::deprecated(),
  probs = lifecycle::deprecated(),
  ...
)

log_lik(object, ...)

# S3 method for class 'mcpfit'
log_lik(
  object,
  newdata = NULL,
  summary = FALSE,
  width = 0.95,
  prior = FALSE,
  group_effects = TRUE,
  arma = TRUE,
  ndraws = NULL,
  draws_format = "matrix",
  nsamples = lifecycle::deprecated(),
  samples_format = lifecycle::deprecated(),
  varying = lifecycle::deprecated(),
  probs = lifecycle::deprecated(),
  ...
)

# S3 method for class 'mcpfit'
residuals(
  object,
  newdata = NULL,
  summary = TRUE,
  width = 0.95,
  prior = FALSE,
  group_effects = TRUE,
  arma = TRUE,
  ndraws = NULL,
  draws_format = "tidy",
  nsamples = lifecycle::deprecated(),
  varying = lifecycle::deprecated(),
  probs = lifecycle::deprecated(),
  ...
)

Arguments

object

An mcpfit object.

newdata

A tibble or a data.frame containing predictors in the model.

  • If NULL (default), the original data is used.

  • Grouping factors must only contain levels from the fitted data. Use group_effects = FALSE to predict without group-level effects, e.g., for new groups.

  • For models with ar() or ma(): fitted(), residuals(), log_lik(), and predict() condition on the response history by default, so newdata must include the response. For fitted(), predict(), and residuals(), missing response histories are supported only in the original fitted data, using retained posterior imputations as histories. Predictions are fresh response draws, including at missing rows. With arma = "replicate", predict() and posterior_predict() generate fresh response series recursively, so their newdata need only contain predictors and required response auxiliaries. log_lik() is unavailable when a missing response enters a later observed history.

  • For models with y | weights(): Require the weights column except for fitted() and predict().

summary

Logical. Summarise the draws for each row in newdata (TRUE) or return the draws (FALSE)?

width

Width of the central interval (strictly between 0 and 1), returned in the .lower and .upper columns. FALSE omits the interval. Only in effect when summary == TRUE. To get custom quantiles, summarise the draws from summary = FALSE, e.g., using dplyr::reframe() (see examples).

rate

Logical scalar. For binomial models, return counts (rate = FALSE, the default for fitted() and predict()) or the observed or expected success proportion (rate = TRUE). Predictions and count-scale fitted values require a trials column in newdata. Distributional parameters such as dpar = "mu" evaluate the parameter itself (e.g., success probability) and are unaffected by rate. Other families do not support rate = TRUE. For rates per unit of exposure in models with offset(log(exposure)), set exposure = 1 in newdata.

prior

Logical. Evaluate prior draws (TRUE) instead of posterior draws (FALSE, default). The selected draws must be available; prior-only fits require prior = TRUE.

group_effects

Group-level effects to include. One of:

  • TRUE All group-level deviations.

  • FALSE or NA No group-level deviations, i.e., population-level predictions. Like re_formula = NA in {brms}.

  • "cp" or "predictor": All group-level deviations belonging to that part of the model.

  • Character vector of group-level parameter names, e.g., c("cp_1_id", "x_2_id"). * is a wildcard, e.g., "state*_1_id" selects all levels of a factor and "*_id" selects all effects by id. See names using ranef(fit). Can be combined, e.g., c("cp", "sigma_*").

arma

How to include AR and MA effects.

  • TRUE: Condition on the observed response history, i.e., one-step-ahead evaluation of the GARMA residual recurrence. Requires the response variable in newdata.

  • FALSE: Disregard AR and MA effects. For family = gaussian(), predict() uses only sigma for residuals.

  • "replicate": Generate fresh response series recursively instead of conditioning on the observed responses. Only for predictions: predict(), posterior_predict(), and pp_check() (where it is the default). Applies equally to prior and posterior draws.

For posterior evaluation of the original data, retained JAGS imputations supply missing GARMA histories. In models with group-level effects, this currently requires all such effects (group_effects = TRUE).

ndraws

Integer or NULL. Number of posterior draws to return/summarise. NULL means "all". More draws trade speed for accuracy.

draws_format

One of "tidy" or "matrix". Controls the output format when summary == FALSE.

nsamples

Deprecated. Use ndraws instead.

samples_format

Deprecated. Use draws_format instead.

varying

Deprecated. Use group_effects instead.

probs

Deprecated. Use width instead.

...

Must be empty. Reserved for future use.

dpar

What distributional parameter to evaluate. E.g.,

  • "epred" (default): Expected response from the full model (or NULL for compatibility with brms etc.).

  • "mu": The conditional mean (or success probability per trial for binomial/bernoulli models), on the link or response scale.

  • "sigma": The standard deviation of the residuals.

  • "ar1", "ar2", "ma1", "ma2", etc. depending on which AR or MA coefficient you want to evaluate.

scale

One of

  • "response": return on the response scale, i.e., after applying the inverse link function.

  • "linear": return on the linear-predictor (link) scale, where the linear trends are modeled.

Value

  • If summary = TRUE: A tibble with the columns of newdata (or fit$data if newdata is NULL), followed by summaries for each row:

    • .mean: The mean of the draws.

    • .sd: The SD of the draws. With posterior draws (the default), this is the posterior predictive SD for predict() and the posterior SD of the evaluated quantity otherwise.

    • .lower and .upper: The lower and upper ends of the central interval given in width.

    For predict() with built-in families, these are the exact moments and quantiles of the posterior predictive distribution (the mixture over posterior draws), so they do not vary with the seed.

    With prior = TRUE, these are the analogous prior summaries. mcp's own columns are dot-prefixed to avoid collisions with data columns.

  • If summary = FALSE and draws_format = "tidy": A tidybayes tibble with all the posterior draws (Nd) evaluated at each row in newdata (Nn), i.e., with Nd x Nn rows, ordered by .row and then .draw. If there are group-level effects, the returned data is expanded with the relevant levels for each row.

    The return columns are:

    • Predictors from newdata, plus its response column when supplied.

    • Draw descriptors: ".chain", ".iteration", ".draw" (see the posterior and tidybayes packages), and .row, the row number in the evaluated newdata.

    • Draw values: one column for each parameter in the model.

    • The estimate (matching tidybayes conventions): .epred for expected responses, .linpred with scale = "linear", the .dpar for other dpars (e.g., .mu or .sigma), .prediction, .residual, or .loglik.

  • If summary = FALSE and draws_format = "matrix": An N_draws X nrows(newdata) matrix with fitted/predicted values (depending on the function). This format is used by brms and it's useful as yrep in bayesplot::ppc_* functions.

Details

fitted() and posterior_epred() evaluate the same expected responses; predict() and posterior_predict() evaluate the same response distributions. The posterior_*() methods return draws-by-observation matrices, while fitted() and predict() summarise by default and also offer tidy draws. For binomial models, the default response scale is counts. Use rate = TRUE for proportions or fitted(..., dpar = "mu") for success probabilities. During migration from v0.3.4, an omitted rate warns once per session per function when counts differ from proportions. Explicit rate settings do not warn.

residuals(fit) is equivalent to fit$data[[mcp_columns(fit)$response]] - fitted(fit, ...) (or newdata[[mcp_columns(fit)$response]] - fitted(fit, ...)), but with fixed arguments for fitted: rate = FALSE, dpar = 'epred'.

log_lik() defaults to an unsummarised draws-by-observation matrix, as used by loo and other posterior workflows. Non-default group_effects and arma settings evaluate conditional or counterfactual log-likelihoods (e.g., without group-level effects or serial correlation); they cannot be used in loo() or waic() because estimating information criteria for reduced models requires refitting.

Missing responses in the original data remain missing in the response column. fitted() returns their expected responses, while predict() generates fresh posterior predictive response draws (including at missing rows). In GARMA models, retained JAGS imputations supply the history used for later fitted and predicted rows. Read more.

Functions

  • predict(mcpfit): Predictive Distribution

  • fitted(mcpfit): Expected response

  • log_lik(mcpfit): Pointwise log-likelihood

  • residuals(mcpfit): Residual distribution

Examples

head(fitted(demo_fit))  # Expected response for each row of demo_fit$data
#> # A tibble: 6 × 6
#>   response  time .mean   .sd .lower .upper
#>      <dbl> <dbl> <dbl> <dbl>  <dbl>  <dbl>
#> 1    12.2   76.3  12.9 1.01   10.9    14.8
#> 2     6.35  83.5  11.4 0.717   9.96   12.8
#> 3    28.0   60.2  25.4 0.873  23.7    27.3
#> 4    15.7   74.7  13.2 1.11   11.0    15.4
#> 5    16.2   85.9  10.9 0.711   9.51   12.3
#> 6    22.3   40.1  14.5 0.621  13.2    15.6
head(residuals(demo_fit))  # Residuals for each row of demo_fit$data
#> # A tibble: 6 × 6
#>   response  time  .mean   .sd .lower .upper
#>      <dbl> <dbl>  <dbl> <dbl>  <dbl>  <dbl>
#> 1    12.2   76.3 -0.645 1.01  -2.54    1.38
#> 2     6.35  83.5 -5.05  0.717 -6.43   -3.61
#> 3    28.0   60.2  2.61  0.873  0.784   4.33
#> 4    15.7   74.7  2.47  1.11   0.327   4.71
#> 5    16.2   85.9  5.30  0.711  3.89    6.70
#> 6    22.3   40.1  7.83  0.621  6.68    9.14
log_lik(demo_fit)[1:3, 1:3]  # Log-likelihood at each demo_fit$data
#>              1         2         3
#> [1,] -2.193497 -3.449599 -2.445390
#> [2,] -2.317434 -3.373387 -2.342121
#> [3,] -2.311202 -3.090324 -2.419474

# All of the above take a range of arguments. E.g.,:
# \donttest{
head(predict(demo_fit))  # Pointwise posterior predictive
#> # A tibble: 6 × 6
#>   response  time .mean   .sd .lower .upper
#>      <dbl> <dbl> <dbl> <dbl>  <dbl>  <dbl>
#> 1    12.2   76.3  12.9  4.00   5.01   20.7
#> 2     6.35  83.5  11.4  3.94   3.65   19.1
#> 3    28.0   60.2  25.4  3.97  17.6    33.2
#> 4    15.7   74.7  13.2  4.03   5.29   21.1
#> 5    16.2   85.9  10.9  3.94   3.17   18.6
#> 6    22.3   40.1  14.5  3.92   6.79   22.2
head(predict(demo_fit, width = 0.8))  # 80% posterior predictive interval
#> # A tibble: 6 × 6
#>   response  time .mean   .sd .lower .upper
#>      <dbl> <dbl> <dbl> <dbl>  <dbl>  <dbl>
#> 1    12.2   76.3  12.9  4.00   7.77   18.0
#> 2     6.35  83.5  11.4  3.94   6.37   16.4
#> 3    28.0   60.2  25.4  3.97  20.4    30.5
#> 4    15.7   74.7  13.2  4.03   8.07   18.4
#> 5    16.2   85.9  10.9  3.94   5.88   15.9
#> 6    22.3   40.1  14.5  3.92   9.49   19.5
head(predict(demo_fit, prior = TRUE))  # Prior predictive
#> # A tibble: 6 × 6
#>   response  time .mean   .sd .lower .upper
#>      <dbl> <dbl> <dbl> <dbl>  <dbl>  <dbl>
#> 1    12.2   76.3  13.5  29.3  -42.7   76.7
#> 2     6.35  83.5  13.4  30.8  -46.6   81.2
#> 3    28.0   60.2  13.5  26.4  -37.9   68.0
#> 4    15.7   74.7  13.7  29.2  -41.0   76.2
#> 5    16.2   85.9  13.0  31.2  -48.3   80.8
#> 6    22.3   40.1  13.7  22.5  -31.2   55.4
head(fitted(demo_fit, summary = FALSE))  # Draws. Useful for plotting distributions.
#> # A tibble: 6 × 14
#>   response  time  .row .chain .iteration .draw  cp_1  cp_2 Intercept_1 time_2 Intercept_3  time_3 sigma_1 .epred
#>      <dbl> <dbl> <int>  <int>      <int> <int> <dbl> <dbl>       <dbl>  <dbl>       <dbl>   <dbl>   <dbl>  <dbl>
#> 1     12.2  76.3     1      1          1     1  31.9  71.0        8.95  0.584        13.9 -0.155     3.48   13.0
#> 2     12.2  76.3     1      1          2     2  31.7  71.4        9.87  0.566        15.8 -0.335     3.47   14.2
#> 3     12.2  76.3     1      1          3     3  32.1  70.5       11.4   0.526        12.6 -0.0956    4.02   12.1
#> 4     12.2  76.3     1      1          4     4  33.3  72.8       10.1   0.561        13.7 -0.174     3.98   13.1
#> 5     12.2  76.3     1      1          5     5  31.7  69.9        9.97  0.466        13.8 -0.158     4.65   12.8
#> 6     12.2  76.3     1      1          6     6  33.3  69.9       10.0   0.536        12.5 -0.140     3.98   11.6
head(fitted(demo_fit, dpar = "sigma"))  # Another model parameter
#> # A tibble: 6 × 6
#>   response  time .mean   .sd .lower .upper
#>      <dbl> <dbl> <dbl> <dbl>  <dbl>  <dbl>
#> 1    12.2   76.3  3.86 0.293   3.34   4.54
#> 2     6.35  83.5  3.86 0.293   3.34   4.54
#> 3    28.0   60.2  3.86 0.293   3.34   4.54
#> 4    15.7   74.7  3.86 0.293   3.34   4.54
#> 5    16.2   85.9  3.86 0.293   3.34   4.54
#> 6    22.3   40.1  3.86 0.293   3.34   4.54

# Custom quantiles from the draws, here for fitted().
# Note that for predict(), this adds more Monte Carlo error than `width`.
fitted(demo_fit, summary = FALSE) |>
  dplyr::group_by(.row, time) |>
  dplyr::reframe(quantile = c(0.1, 0.5, 0.9), .epred = quantile(.epred, quantile)) |>
  head()
#> # A tibble: 6 × 4
#>    .row  time quantile .epred
#>   <int> <dbl>    <dbl>  <dbl>
#> 1     1  76.3      0.1   11.6
#> 2     1  76.3      0.5   12.8
#> 3     1  76.3      0.9   14.2
#> 4     2  83.5      0.1   10.5
#> 5     2  83.5      0.5   11.4
#> 6     2  83.5      0.9   12.3

# Evaluate at novel data
novel_data = data.frame(time = c(-5, 20, 300))  # Only predictors are needed
head(predict(demo_fit, newdata = novel_data))
#> # A tibble: 3 × 5
#>    time  .mean   .sd .lower .upper
#>   <dbl>  <dbl> <dbl>  <dbl>  <dbl>
#> 1    -5   9.97  3.93   2.25  17.7 
#> 2    20   9.97  3.93   2.25  17.7 
#> 3   300 -33.2  18.4  -69.9    2.39

# Work with missing responses
missing_fit = mcp_example("missing", plot = FALSE)
#> NA values detected in 'y'. JAGS will treat them as latent responses and impute them during sampling.
fitted(missing_fit) |> dplyr::filter(is.na(y)) |> head()  # Expected responses for missing y
#> # A tibble: 6 × 7
#>       y     x state .mean   .sd .lower .upper
#>   <dbl> <int> <fct> <dbl> <dbl>  <dbl>  <dbl>

fitted(missing_fit, summary = FALSE) |> dplyr::filter(is.na(y)) |> head()  # Same, but draws

#>       y     x state  .row .chain .iteration .draw  cp_1 Intercept_1   x_1 stateB_1    x_2 sigma_1 .epred

#> 6    NA     8 B         8      1          6     6  58.5        11.9 0.183     21.8 -0.424    4.29   35.2
predict(missing_fit) |> dplyr::filter(is.na(y)) |> head()  # Posterior predictive for missing y
